newsitem.title: USA: Central bank 1997 gold sales seen at 10m/oz - CPM.
newsitem.headline: Central bank 1997 gold sales seen at 10m/oz - CPM.

text.p: Net sales of gold by central banks are forecast at 10 million ounces in 1996 and could amount to 10 million ounces again next year, CPM Group managing director Jeffrey Christian said Thursday.
"These sales are not expected to disrupt the gold market though," Christian told analysts attending the research company's annual gold market briefing.
"Perhaps more important, there are no indications that central banks are pulling back from the market," Christian said.
"Central bank gold leasing activity has increased significantly over the past 14 years and could double in the next eight years or so," he said.
Included in the forecast for sales of 10 million ounces next year is a sale of about two million ounces of gold by the IMF.
Under a current proposal, the IMF may sell about five million ounces of its 103 million ounce gold reserve over the next five years to finance its third world debt relief plan.
Through August 1996 net reported official disposals totaled 4.18 million ounces, CPM Group said in its "Gold Survey 1996", published Tuesday.

The bulk of this 4.81 million ounces represents the 5.22 million ounces sold by Belgium early this year, but in addition to the Belgian sale, seven other countries have reported selling 810,000 ounces in the first half.
Most of these sales have been by central banks that buy domestic gold mine output, such as Brazil, Russia, South Africa, Zimbabwe and the Philippines.
The U.S. reported adding 10,000 ounces to its reserve, to replace gold lent to the U.S. Mint for use in gold coins.

However, Christian downplayed rumors European central banks would increase gold sales in an attempt to help their countries reach the debt-to-GDP ratios needed to qualify for membership in the European Monetary union and single currency program due to begin in 1999.

"The debt criteria have to be met by 1997 for EMU qualification and there's no way European countries could sell enough gold to reduce their debts to meet the targets, so this won't be a reason for European bank sales," Christian said.

"Despite rumors to the contrary, gold backed bonds issued by the the new European Monetary Institute (EMI), to support the single currency, are also unlikely for political reasons as it would imply less confidence in the new currency than in existing currencies," he said.
The EMI, the precursor to a future single European central bank, currently holds 92.1 million ounces of gold, CPM said.

Gold held on behalf of foreign governments at the New York Federal Reserve has declined steadily in the past decade from around 340 million ounces to 270 million currently as central bank leasing activity has forced gold reserves out into other depositaries such as the Bank of England and private depositaries, Christian said.
CPM Group now estimates that at any given time there is between 25 and 50 million ounces of gold lent out by central banks.
At least 43 central banks are believed to be active in the gold lending business which includes gold loans, swaps, repos, and option programs.
